reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 10, Reshaping Data in PostgreSQL. Reshaping changes structure, not the underlying facts. We will move between long and wide forms, pivot categories into columns, unpivot columns back into rows, preserve meaningful NULL values, and protect the intended analytical grain. The most important habit in this module is to say what one output row represents before you write the reshape query. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a BI dashboard turning monthly categories into presentation columns. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Reshaping changes structure
slides.transcript: Long and wide are not quality levels. They are different ways to arrange information. Long data usually stores categories as row values. Wide data turns selected category values into columns. The dangerous part is that many pivots also aggregate. When several source rows map to one pivot cell, detail may be permanently removed. Connect this idea to a machine-learning workflow converting wide measurements into tidy long data. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you should be able to identify long and wide structures, pivot and unpivot data in PostgreSQL, and explain the grain of each result. You should also be able to detect when a reshape changes more than structure because aggregation or a join has altered the facts. Finally, you should be able to choose a shape based on what happens next: visualization, reporting, or modeling. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a survey project reshaping question responses for analysis. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript: The module starts with the shape itself. Then we will pivot long data to wide form. After that, we will unpivot wide data back to long form. Next comes the most important safeguard: grain. Finally, we validate totals and choose the output shape that best serves the downstream use. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a BI dashboard turning monthly categories into presentation columns. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript: The teaching database includes several examples because reshaping appears in many domains. Admissions and sales begin in long form. Monthly sales and patient metrics begin in wide form. Survey responses and grades are useful for matrix-style pivots. The different examples help you focus on the reshape pattern rather than memorizing one dataset. Connect this idea to a machine-learning workflow converting wide measurements into tidy long data. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Long form
slides.transcript: In long form, the month is stored as a value in a column. Laptop January and Laptop February occupy different rows. This shape is flexible because a new month can simply become another row. Long form is common for time-series analysis, plotting, grouping, and tidy analytical workflows. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Wide form
slides.transcript: In wide form, January and February are separate columns. Now one row represents a product rather than a product-month. This can be convenient for scorecards, matrices, and fixed reports. The same business relationship is being displayed differently, but the row grain has changed. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Same facts, different shape
slides.transcript: These two tables represent the same simplified information. The long table has one product-month per row. The wide table has one product per row. Before reshaping, state both grains clearly. That makes it easier to identify what has changed and whether any information has been aggregated away. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: What is grain?
slides.transcript: Grain means what one row represents. A sales fact table may have one row per transaction. After grouping, the grain may become one product-month. After pivoting months into columns, the grain may become one product. If you cannot state the row grain, it is difficult to know whether a reshape is correct. Reshaping can change grain, so define it before and after the transformation. A source may have one row per patient-measurement, while a pivoted result has one row per patient. If multiple source rows map to the same target cell, you must decide how they are aggregated; otherwise information can be lost.

slides.title: State grain before SQL
slides.transcript: Before writing a pivot, complete one sentence: one output row represents what? Once the row meaning is clear, identify which category values should become columns. Then identify the measure that belongs in each cell. Finally ask whether several source rows can map to the same cell. If they can, you need an aggregation rule. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a BI dashboard turning monthly categories into presentation columns, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Prefer long form when
slides.transcript: Long form is often the more flexible analytical shape. If categories change frequently, new values simply appear in rows. Long form also works naturally with trend charts, filtering, grouping, and many modeling workflows. It avoids changing the schema every time a new category appears. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Prefer wide form when
slides.transcript: Wide form is useful when categories are stable and users want side-by-side comparison. A scorecard with January, February, and March columns is easy to scan. A grade matrix can place courses in fixed columns. But wide schemas become harder to maintain when categories change frequently. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Reshaping is not always only reshaping
slides.transcript: A pivot often requires aggregation. If only one source row maps to each output cell, the reshape can preserve that value directly. But if multiple source rows map to one cell, PostgreSQL needs an aggregate such as SUM, COUNT, MAX, or AVG. That aggregation changes the level of detail, so it must be chosen deliberately. Connect this idea to a BI dashboard turning monthly categories into presentation columns. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Inspect long admissions
slides.transcript: Before pivoting admissions, inspect the long source. Each admission is a row. Diagnosis is stored as a value, not as a column. The pivot will create separate diagnosis count columns by month. Understanding the source grain makes the later GROUP BY easier to interpret. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Pivot mental model
slides.transcript: A pivot can be planned with four decisions. First, define the output row grain. Second, identify the category values that should become columns. Third, choose the measure. Fourth, choose the aggregate needed to fill each cell. For the diagnosis example, one output row is one month, the categories are diagnoses, and the measure is admission count. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Conditional aggregation
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL does not require a special PIVOT keyword for the core patterns taught here. You can use conditional aggregation. One common form is SUM with CASE. PostgreSQL also supports FILTER on aggregate functions, which can be very readable. Both approaches use the same underlying idea: one grouped output row with category-specific aggregate columns. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Pivot with CASE
slides.transcript: This query groups admissions by month. Inside each SUM, CASE contributes one when the row matches a selected diagnosis and zero otherwise. The sum becomes the diagnosis count for that month. Run the query and verify that each result row represents one month. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Read the CASE pivot
slides.transcript: In the CASE pivot, each output measure has a different condition. The GROUP BY defines one output row per month. Inside that month, each SUM looks only at rows belonging to its diagnosis category. This separation between row grain and category condition is the core pivot pattern. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Pivot with FILTER
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL FILTER attaches a condition directly to an aggregate. COUNT star FILTER where diagnosis equals Pneumonia counts only matching rows. The query is often easier to scan because the aggregate and its condition appear together. Run it and compare the result with the CASE version. The output should express the same business meaning. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: CASE vs FILTER
slides.transcript: CASE and FILTER are two styles for conditional aggregation. CASE is broadly portable and flexible. FILTER is particularly readable in PostgreSQL when you want category-specific counts or sums. Choose the form that is clear for the environment you are using. The output grain and aggregate meaning matter more than the stylistic choice. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Pivot revenue
slides.transcript: A pivot can aggregate revenue instead of counts. This query groups by sale month. Each filtered SUM collects revenue for one product. The result has one row per month and separate revenue columns for Laptop, Mouse, and Keyboard. Always identify both the output grain and the measure being aggregated. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Pivot survey responses
slides.transcript: Survey data often arrives in long form with one row per respondent-question. If there is at most one score for each respondent and question, MAX can be used as a convenient aggregate to place that value into the correct column. The output grain becomes one respondent. The Q1, Q2, and Q3 categories become columns. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: NULL and zero are different
slides.transcript: An empty pivot cell should not automatically become zero. NULL may mean no observation was recorded. Zero may mean the observation exists and its measured value is zero. Those are different facts. Before using ELSE zero or COALESCE, decide what an absent source row means for the analytical question. After reshaping, NULL and zero may have very different meanings. NULL can mean the category did not occur or was not measured; zero can mean it was measured and the value was truly zero. Do not replace NULL with zero unless that interpretation is correct for the business question.

slides.title: NULL semantics example
slides.transcript: This example shows two versions of the same pivot cell. The first CASE has no ELSE zero, so a missing Q3 response stays NULL. The second explicitly forces zero. Run the query and find respondents with no Q3 observation. Ask whether zero is a real score or simply a convenient placeholder. That distinction affects later averages and models. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a survey project reshaping question responses for analysis, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Validate pivot totals
slides.transcript: A reshape should be validated. For additive measures such as revenue, calculate the total from the source. Then calculate the total represented by the pivot cells. The totals should agree when the same observations are included. This simple check catches many grouping and join mistakes. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Inspect a wide source
slides.transcript: Now we reverse the direction. The monthly sales table stores January, February, and March as separate columns. That is convenient for a fixed report, but less flexible for many analytical tasks. Unpivoting turns those month columns back into row values. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Unpivot mental model
slides.transcript: Unpivoting converts repeated measure columns into rows. The wide source has one product row with several month columns. The long result will have a month column and a revenue column. The row grain changes from one product to one product-month. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Method 1: UNION ALL
slides.transcript: UNION ALL is a straightforward unpivot pattern. Write one SELECT for each source column. Give each SELECT the same output structure. Then stack the rows with UNION ALL. This is verbose but very beginner-friendly because each source column is visible in its own SELECT. Unpivoting turns repeated columns into row values. UNION ALL is explicit and portable; LATERAL VALUES can be more compact in PostgreSQL. The important design decision is which columns become identifiers and which column names become values. Keep data types compatible across the generated rows.

slides.title: Unpivot with UNION ALL
slides.transcript: This query produces three SELECT blocks. Each one assigns a month date and uses the corresponding wide revenue column. UNION ALL stacks the results. Run it and verify that one product row has expanded into multiple product-month rows. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Method 2: LATERAL VALUES
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL offers a compact unpivot pattern with CROSS JOIN LATERAL and VALUES. For each monthly sales row, VALUES creates several month-revenue pairs. LATERAL allows those pairs to reference jan revenue, feb revenue, and mar revenue from the current source row. This is often cleaner than repeating full SELECT statements. Unpivoting turns repeated columns into row values. UNION ALL is explicit and portable; LATERAL VALUES can be more compact in PostgreSQL. The important design decision is which columns become identifiers and which column names become values. Keep data types compatible across the generated rows.

slides.title: Unpivot with LATERAL VALUES
slides.transcript: This query keeps the source table once. The lateral VALUES block emits three rows for each product. Each generated row contains a sale month and the corresponding revenue. Run the query and compare the output with UNION ALL. The two forms should represent the same long relationship. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: UNION ALL vs LATERAL
slides.transcript: Both methods are useful. UNION ALL is explicit and easy to read when there are only a few columns. LATERAL VALUES is compact when many columns follow the same repeated structure. The correct choice is the one that keeps the transformation clear and maintainable. Unpivoting turns repeated columns into row values. UNION ALL is explicit and portable; LATERAL VALUES can be more compact in PostgreSQL. The important design decision is which columns become identifiers and which column names become values. Keep data types compatible across the generated rows.

slides.title: Unpivot patient metrics
slides.transcript: Patient metrics provides another unpivot example. Heart rate, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and oxygen saturation are separate wide columns. The lateral VALUES block converts them into metric and value rows. This can be useful for generic plotting, rule processing, or feature inspection. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Common type requirement
slides.transcript: When several source columns become one value column, PostgreSQL needs a common data type. If one metric is integer and another is numeric, explicit casts may be helpful. The patient metric example casts selected values to numeric. Do not let type coercion become an accidental part of the reshape. Choose the long value type deliberately. Connect this idea to a BI dashboard turning monthly categories into presentation columns. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Preserve or drop NULL cells
slides.transcript: Unpivoting raises a NULL-policy question. You can preserve rows whose value is NULL. That keeps the category present and marks the measurement missing. Or you can drop NULL rows after unpivoting. The right choice depends on whether missingness itself matters to the analysis. After reshaping, NULL and zero may have very different meanings. NULL can mean the category did not occur or was not measured; zero can mean it was measured and the value was truly zero. Do not replace NULL with zero unless that interpretation is correct for the business question.

slides.title: Drop NULL after unpivot
slides.transcript: This query uses the lateral VALUES pattern and then filters out rows whose generated revenue is NULL. The WHERE clause makes the policy explicit. Run it and compare the row count with a version that keeps all generated rows. Always document whether missing cells were preserved or removed. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Round trip
slides.transcript: A reshape round trip is not automatically reversible. If the pivot aggregated transaction rows to monthly totals, unpivoting can only recover those monthly totals. It cannot recreate the original transaction IDs or individual amounts. The grain that survives is the aggregated grain. A reshape is reversible only when the transformation preserves enough information to reconstruct the source. Aggregation, duplicate collapsing, and dropped NULL cells can make the process lossy. Validate row counts, keys, totals, and category coverage before assuming a pivot-unpivot round trip preserves everything.

slides.title: Round-trip SQL
slides.transcript: This query first creates a wide product-level table with month totals. Then it unpivots the wide columns into product-month rows. The result is long again, but it is not the original transaction table. It is one row per product-month total. That is the key distinction between reshaping and recovering detail. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a machine-learning workflow converting wide measurements into tidy long data, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Reversible vs lossy
slides.transcript: A reshape is more reversible when each source value maps cleanly to one output cell and category labels are preserved. It becomes lossy when several rows are aggregated into one cell. Dropping NULL rows can also remove missingness information. Collapsing categories can remove distinctions. Always identify which information survives the transformation. A reshape is reversible only when the transformation preserves enough information to reconstruct the source. Aggregation, duplicate collapsing, and dropped NULL cells can make the process lossy. Validate row counts, keys, totals, and category coverage before assuming a pivot-unpivot round trip preserves everything.

slides.title: Grain is the safeguard
slides.transcript: The seeded sales table intentionally contains multiple Laptop transactions in January. A product by month pivot has only one Laptop January cell. That means the two transaction rows must be combined. If the measure is revenue, SUM is a reasonable choice. But the transaction-level detail is no longer present in that cell. Reshaping can change grain, so define it before and after the transformation. A source may have one row per patient-measurement, while a pivoted result has one row per patient. If multiple source rows map to the same target cell, you must decide how they are aggregated; otherwise information can be lost.

slides.title: Check source grain
slides.transcript: This query groups the sales source by product and month. COUNT tells us how many transaction rows exist in each product-month group. SUM shows the total revenue that would fill a pivot cell. Look for groups where source rows is greater than one. Those groups prove that the pivot requires aggregation. Reshaping can change grain, so define it before and after the transformation. A source may have one row per patient-measurement, while a pivoted result has one row per patient. If multiple source rows map to the same target cell, you must decide how they are aggregated; otherwise information can be lost.

slides.title: See information loss
slides.transcript: The first query shows the individual Laptop January sale rows. The second query sums them into one product-month value. That one total can be placed into a pivot cell. But after aggregation, the individual sale IDs and amounts cannot be recovered from the total alone. This is the detail lost by aggregation. A reshape is reversible only when the transformation preserves enough information to reconstruct the source. Aggregation, duplicate collapsing, and dropped NULL cells can make the process lossy. Validate row counts, keys, totals, and category coverage before assuming a pivot-unpivot round trip preserves everything.

slides.title: Join before pivot carefully
slides.transcript: Reshaping often happens after joins. The danger is that a join can multiply fact rows. If you join a patient dimension to admissions, the admission grain can remain intact. But joining admissions to another one-to-many child table can create repeated admission combinations. Always check cardinality before pivoting joined data. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Patient admissions by month
slides.transcript: This query starts from patients and left joins admissions. The patient table contributes one descriptive row per patient. Admissions provides the events being counted. Filtered counts create January, February, and March admission columns. The GROUP BY keeps one output row per patient. Because the join relationship is understood, the counts remain meaningful. Connect this idea to a machine-learning workflow converting wide measurements into tidy long data. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: One-to-many multiplication risk
slides.transcript: The important question is whether the join preserves the measure's fact grain. A many-to-one lookup often preserves the fact rows. A broad join between two fact-like tables can multiply them. If rows are already duplicated before the pivot, the pivot aggregates inflated facts. Check row counts and key relationships first. Joining detail tables before reshaping can multiply rows. If the target is one row per patient or product, summarize each one-to-many source to the target grain before combining them. This keeps measures interpretable and prevents a pivot from hiding earlier join inflation.

slides.title: Pre-aggregate before reshaping
slides.transcript: Pre-aggregation can help control grain. First summarize the fact table to the level you actually need. Then perform later joins or pivots from that stable grain. This separates fact aggregation from presentation reshaping and can make the query easier to verify. Joining detail tables before reshaping can multiply rows. If the target is one row per patient or product, summarize each one-to-many source to the target grain before combining them. This keeps measures interpretable and prevents a pivot from hiding earlier join inflation.

slides.title: Pre-aggregate sales
slides.transcript: The CTE first creates one row per product, category, and month. The outer query then groups by category and creates month columns. So there are two grain changes. Run the query and state both of them. Being explicit about intermediate grain is one of the best protections against accidental double counting. Joining detail tables before reshaping can multiply rows. If the target is one row per patient or product, summarize each one-to-many source to the target grain before combining them. This keeps measures interpretable and prevents a pivot from hiding earlier join inflation.

slides.title: Dynamic categories
slides.transcript: Wide pivot columns are part of the schema. If the categories are stable, that is manageable. If new products or diagnoses appear frequently, the SQL must change to add columns. Long form handles dynamic categories more naturally because new categories become new rows. Often a BI tool can create the presentation matrix from long data. Static pivots are easier to read and validate when the category set is known. Dynamic pivots are useful when categories change, but they introduce schema variability that downstream dashboards or models must handle. Discover categories first and decide whether a changing column set is acceptable.

slides.title: Discover categories first
slides.transcript: Before creating a static pivot, inspect the category values. This script lists distinct diagnoses and products. If the current data includes categories you did not plan for, a fixed pivot may omit them. Discovery helps make the schema decision explicit. Connect this idea to a BI dashboard turning monthly categories into presentation columns. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Static category pivot
slides.transcript: This static pivot creates three diagnosis columns. It works well when those categories are intentionally selected and stable. The advantage is a predictable schema. The limitation is that any new diagnosis category will not automatically appear as a new column. A pivot converts category values into columns, usually through conditional aggregation in portable SQL. Each target column needs a clear aggregation rule. Before pivoting, check whether the source contains more than one value for the same row-key and category combination.

slides.title: Optional crosstab
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL has an optional crosstab function through the tablefunc extension. It can create pivot tables, but it requires extension support and explicit output-column definitions. For this course, conditional aggregation is the core pattern because it is transparent and works well in the browser environment. You can explore crosstab later for selected reporting scenarios. Static pivots are easier to read and validate when the category set is known. Dynamic pivots are useful when categories change, but they introduce schema variability that downstream dashboards or models must handle. Discover categories first and decide whether a changing column set is acceptable.

slides.title: Choose shape for the next task
slides.transcript: There is no universally best shape. A fixed dashboard matrix may be easier to read in wide form. A trend chart usually benefits from long form because the category and time dimensions stay as values. Choose the shape based on the next analytical or reporting task. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Long result for charting
slides.transcript: This query creates a long monthly product summary. Each row represents one product-month. The time dimension, category dimension, and measure stay in separate columns. This shape is flexible for charting because new products become new rows instead of requiring new columns. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Long vs wide downstream
slides.transcript: Reshaping should be driven by the downstream consumer. Long form is often more robust for charts, modeling, and changing categories. Wide form is useful for fixed business reports and interfaces. A good pipeline can keep a reusable long analytical table and create wide presentation outputs only where needed. Long and wide are not labels for good and bad design; they are shapes suited to different tasks. Long data is often easier for grouping, plotting, and scalable storage. Wide data is often convenient for human-readable reports or some modeling interfaces. Choose the shape required by the next step.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.transcript: Practice 1 reshapes student grades. The source is long: one student-course grade per row. The output should have one row per student and fixed course columns. A missing course should remain NULL because no recorded grade is not the same as a grade of zero. For this activity, make a prediction before you run anything. State what one output row should represent, which records you expect to remain, and what edge case is most likely to expose a mistake. Then run the SQL and compare the result with that prediction. slides.title: Module 10 takeaways
slides.transcript: These are the key habits from Module 10. State the grain first. Use conditional aggregation for pivots. Use UNION ALL or lateral VALUES for unpivoting. slides.title: Reshaping decision guide
slides.transcript: Use this guide when deciding how to reshape. If category values should become columns, pivot with conditional aggregation. If columns should become rows, use UNION ALL or lateral VALUES. Keep dynamic categories long when possible. Use a wide form for stable matrix reporting.
